shorts.description:
A stranger messaged me for encouraging words as his father had passed away the night before.

Here’s what I sent:

Be the man he’d want you to be. 

Instead of focusing on your sadness, focus on helping everyone else through theirs.

Use the proximity of his death to get you to take the actions you were too afraid to take before. Because the window of time where his death affects you will be finite. But the changes you make can be everlasting.

If you live his values, he lives on through you.

And ask yourself a scary question: how can this make me better? Then answer it. 

Realize that the length of time you mourn has nothing to do with how much you loved him. 

You don’t have to be sad to prove to yourself that you loved him.
shorts.title: You Only Have Two Hands and One Brain. Use Them.

shorts.description:

shorts.description:

2) Risk: charge more for taking on risk (or eliminating it)

I'm always cycling thru these when trying to add value.

2) Advertise until the timer is up.

shorts.description:
Have you ever thought…

 “I wish I could just fast forward thru this shitty part and get to when my goal becomes real?”

Right. Me too. 

But taken to the natural extreme, the day you die, you would’ve achieved all the goals you set out to accomplish. 

And then - immediately die. 

Which when you think about it - shows how silly it is for us to think this way. 

You might as well say “I’d like to fast forward to the end of the movie”

If that’s the case, you might as well not watch it. Or in our case - live it. 

So - the reverse of that would be to value the shitty part as equal (or even greater than) the end. 

Since we don’t want the story to end (we die), we flip the “fast forward to the end” frame to “slow down right now”

In other words - the todays - become the “good ol days” of our future selves looking back. 

And - doing the work - becomes the only goal worth living for.
shorts.title: At What Point Should You Enjoy the Fruits of Your Labor?
